summary:
On Earth, fire climbs. Heat lifts, air rushes in, and the flame stands tall and gold. In freefall, nothing pulls it upward. The flame turns round and blue, and it can burn quietly where no one sees it, while the real danger, toxic gas, spreads before the smoke appears.

For thirty years, NASA's experiments have mapped this strange behavior, but the knowledge lies scattered across dense papers. The Zero-G Fire Atlas gathers it into one place: 24 sources, 693 cited findings, every number traceable to its page.

Watch a flame change in our interactive Flame Lab. Compare the ISS, the Moon and Mars. Follow crew procedures that keep fires small, detect them early and put them out fast. Ask a question and receive only verified quotes, never invention.

We cannot repeal fire's nature, but we can understand it before it matters.
details:
What it does and how it works
The Zero-G Fire Atlas is an interactive dashboard that turns 24 sources of NASA microgravity fire research into 693 cited findings, each linked to its source page. Users can watch flames change in the Flame Lab, explore ranked insights and mission scenarios (ISS, Moon, Mars), follow crew-procedure guidance in Safety & Ops, and search the data with Ask the Data, which returns only verbatim quotes with citations.

Benefits
It makes scattered research usable in seconds. Every claim is traceable and carries a confidence rating, and Ask the Data never invents facts. It also turns findings into action: smoke was detected 344 s after ignition in Saffire VI-3, so crews must monitor CO and CO₂.

Intended impact
Safer spacecraft and habitats for the Moon and Mars, by helping astronauts and mission planners keep fires small, detect them early and extinguish them fast.

Tools used
Our team carried out the research itself. We used Claude to help brief and summarise that research, and Claude Code for the coding.

Creativity
Flame Lab lets people see fire behave differently by dragging sliders instead of reading papers. Ask the Data deliberately avoids generated text to stay trustworthy, and paper rankings use adjustable weights.

Factors considered
Trust (source realism tags and confidence levels), honesty about limits (Flame Lab is labelled an illustrative model), realistic conditions (ISS air and planned low-pressure, high-oxygen habitats), and the audience, astronauts and mission planners, super intelligence chatbot (Groq by OpenAI)
